tldr: The Neural GPU is a parallel, convolutional gated recurrent unit architecture that learns algorithmic tasks like binary addition and multiplication from examples and generalizes perfectly to inputs far longer than those seen during training.
contributions: Introducing the Neural GPU, a Turing-complete but highly parallel neural network architecture for learning algorithms
Demonstrating the first neural network to learn an algorithm (long binary multiplication) whose runtime is superlinear in input size
Introducing parameter sharing relaxation as a technique for training deep recurrent networks
Showing that small dropout and gradient noise significantly improve learning and generalization
methods: The Neural GPU uses convolutional gated recurrent units (CGRU) operating on a 2D mental image tensor of shape [w=4, h=n, m=24]. Input sequences are embedded into the first column and then processed through l=2 layers of CGRUs applied for n time steps. The final output is read from the first column via a linear output matrix. Training uses the Adam optimizer with gradient clipping, parameter sharing relaxation (r=6), dropout on recurrent connections, gradient noise, and curriculum learning. A grid search over 729 hyperparameter configurations was performed for each experiment.
results: The Neural GPU achieved zero errors on long binary multiplication trained on up to 20-bit numbers and tested on numbers up to 2000 bits long. It also learned long binary addition with no errors, generalizing beyond training length. By comparison, LSTM+A could not learn binary multiplication at all and generalized to only ~25 bits on addition, while stack-RNNs generalized only to ~100 bits on addition. The same architecture solved copying, reversing, duplicating, and counting tasks with perfect generalization up to 4001 bits after training on lengths up to 41.
limitations: Testing was limited by technical implementation constraints to around 2000 bits. The architecture requires extensive grid search (729 runs) to find well-generalizing models. Parameter sharing relaxation increases memory usage when using larger r values. Stack-RNN baselines were trained with a different regime, making direct comparison partially unfair.
